MODULE – I: CONVERSATION
A note on the expressions to be used on certain occasions

While speaking English — or in the spoken form of English — certain expressions are to be used because the English language is very formal and official. As learners and users of English it is necessary that the formal British idiom is learnt to make official deals, and transactions absolutely formal communicative and clear.

In the course of any conversation it is necessary to use the correct idiom, expression and usage without the influence of the mother tongue or vernacular, which includes manners and etiquette. You are expected to be very formal, and behave courteously with manners in any situation, especially while in group discussions etc.
On meeting a person for the first time in the day the usual greeting
Good morning Sir / Madam / Raju etc.
When you meet the same person or any other in the noon
Good afternoon sir / Madam.
When you meet in the evening
Good evening Sir / Madam / Raju.
When you meet your friends, classmates and people of same age group, your greet them
Hello Raju / Remi, How are you?

When you meet a person for the first time or he is introduced by some common friend you say:
I’m glad to meet you. Glad to meet you sir. Nice meeting you — likewise the answer should be the same.
When you are wished by a friend ‘Hello Roy, How are you?’ Your answer should be fine, thank you, how are you?
If its an old friend you have not met for many days — you say, It’s long time since we met. How are things?
or How is everything?
After meeting, your depart, on departing you wish your friends / master / father etc.
Good Bye! Friends. Bye – Bye friends. See you later friends – if it is night time you
Good night.
Some times you may have to seek permission from your superiors.
Will you please excuse me sir. May I leave the room sir. May I answer your questions sir. (When it is not your turn)
Gratitude
Thanks is a very vital aspect of British manners. You say,
Thank you, Sir / Madam. That is very kind of you, Raju. I’m really grateful to you sir, for your timely help.
How do you respond to thanks and gratitude expressed. When someone says, “Thank you, Raju” you say,
That’s all right, Sekar. — or — Not at all, Sekar. — or — It’s a pleasure. — or — Don’t mention it. — or — No mention please. — or — You are most welcome.
(Responding to gratitude and thanks is very normal behavior — don’t
Indianisms or coin your own answer, this is the standard form, stick to it if you want to be correct.)

Some common expressions in English

I am thirsty – I am hungry – I am sleepy – I am happy – I am bored – I feel dull – I am excited – I am contented – I am unhappy – I am sad – I am sorry – I am late – I am in time – I am a doctor – I am a lawyer – I am a software engineer.
These are states of being: Thirsty – hungry – sleepy – happy – bored – dull – excited – content – unhappy – sad – sorry – late.
Framing questions
Framing question in the conservation is a very vital part of communication.
The basic form of a question are direct beginning with question markers viz. What, Where, When, Why, How.
Where do you live?
What brings you here?
Where is the book?
Why are you late?
How old are you?
The basic form of a question — the verb ‘be’ precedes the subject, and in other cases the subject is placed between the auxiliary and main verbs.
Is this a safe vehicle?
Are you accompanying me to see the movie?

In a conversation with a friend or in an official situation, asking straight questions may lack politeness. A friendly approach is needed in a conversation to elicit the right and desired response as shown below.
Friendly questions — Response
Would you mind if I called you up?
— No, not at all. Would you mind helping in the service?
— No, not at all. Would you like to have a cup of coffee?
— Yes, certainly or No Thank you. Could I speak to Dr. Roa please?
— Yes, please do so. Could you tell me your address?
— Yes, I would love to.

A Question is generally asked for seeking information or classification. It has certain other functions as well. Some of them are as follows: Inviting — Would you like to attend the party? Request — Could you lend me your book? Offering help — Could I carry your brief case? Permission — May I come in? Suggestion — Could you change the date of the meeting?

The word order is very important in any question. Avoid translating questions from the vernacular. (The teacher may give suitable examples from the vernacular which influence the framing of questions in English and instruct the students to avoid those pitfalls in the process of a conversation to make communication exact and meaningful.) Differentiate between direct and indirect questions. Direct: Where is the market located? Indirect: Could you tell me the location of the market please?
